By the time four statisticians published the seminal book Classification and Regression Trees in 1984, statisticians had already experimented with algorithms that graphically presented looked like triangle-shaped Christmas trees.

While this series of articles about Decision Trees focuses primarily on the methodological framework covered in the aforementioned book - and eventually on the currently used modern tree-based algorithms we use today, it is worth taking few steps back to the early history of the tree-based methods and how it all began.

**Automatic Interaction Detection (1963)**

Two researchers in the University of Michigan were analyzing US households survey data, and they must have been frustrated by a fundamental limitation of the most commonly used tool of the time: regression, is problematic when the explanatory variables have interactions with each other. They identified additional concerns in their paper, but the issue with interaction effects between the variables was the most striking.
